title: Your UDID Card and What It Unlocks

level-1.title: A card that helps
summary: There is a special card for Deaf and hard-of-hearing people in India. It is called a UDID card.
It shows, anywhere in India, that you are Deaf. You do not have to explain again and again.
The card helps your family get money for school books, hearing aids and travel.
It is free to ask for one. A trusted adult and a government doctor help you get it.
Ask a grown-up at home if you have a UDID card. Many families do not know about it.

questions.prompt: Your family moves to a new state. Without a UDID card, what problem might you face at a new school that the card is specifically designed to solve?

image.alt: A family moving between two states with a school in the new one

options.label: Having to explain and prove that you are Deaf all over again in the new place
Having to pay extra fees in the new state
Not being allowed to enrol in a new school at all

questions.hint: The card's whole purpose is to avoid repeating one particular kind of explanation.

questions.prompt: If the UDID card is free and helps get money for books and hearing aids, why might a family still be missing out on this help?

image.alt: A family who has never heard of the card

options.label: Because they may not know the card exists at all, so they never apply for it
Because the card actually costs too much for most families
Because only certain families are allowed to apply

questions.hint: The lesson names one specific reason many families miss out, and it has nothing to do with cost.

questions.prompt: Someone messages your family claiming they can 'fast-track' your UDID card for a fee, skipping the doctor. What TWO things about this claim contradict the lesson?

image.alt: A suspicious message offering a paid shortcut, skipping a doctor

options.label: The real process is free, and it requires a government doctor, not a shortcut from a stranger
Nothing is wrong, fast-tracking is allowed for a fee
Only the fee is suspicious, the no-doctor part is fine

questions.hint: Compare this offer against both the cost and the correct people involved, from the lesson.

level-2.title: The card, the hearing aid and the pension
summary: The UDID card is the gateway. Almost every other scheme asks for it first, so nothing else starts until you have one.
To get it you need a disability certificate from a government medical board, usually showing 40% or more — what the law calls a benchmark disability.
ADIP is the scheme that pays for equipment: hearing aids, and cochlear implants for people who qualify. It depends on family income and is run through government hospitals, ALIMCO and approved NGOs.
Most states pay a monthly disability pension. The amount is different in every state, and usually needs 40% disability plus income and residence rules.
For families below the poverty line there is also a central pension, IGNDPS, which some states top up.
Travel costs less too — Indian Railways and many state buses give concessions to disabled passengers.
None of this arrives on its own. Somebody has to apply. That is the single most useful thing in this lesson.

questions.prompt: A family has a doctor's note saying their child's hearing loss is 25%. They want to apply for a UDID card. What problem might they run into?

image.alt: A medical note showing twenty-five percent beside a gateway of schemes

options.label: 40% is usually the benchmark needed, so 25% may not qualify them
25% is more than enough, since any percentage qualifies
The percentage does not matter at all for a UDID card

questions.hint: Recall the specific benchmark percentage the lesson mentions.

questions.prompt: A family needs money to buy a hearing aid, and separately, a small amount every month for living costs. Which scheme covers which need, and why?

image.alt: A hearing aid beside a monthly pension payment

options.label: ADIP covers the hearing aid (equipment); a disability pension covers the monthly amount (ongoing support)
ADIP covers both needs entirely on its own
A disability pension pays for equipment, not monthly support

questions.hint: One scheme is about a one-time piece of equipment; the other is about a repeating monthly payment.

questions.prompt: A family qualifies for a state disability pension and has all the right papers, but never actually submitted an application. Will the pension arrive anyway eventually?

image.alt: An unopened envelope beside a pile of qualifying papers

options.label: No — qualifying is not enough; someone must actively apply for it to ever arrive
Yes, the government tracks who qualifies and pays automatically
Only if they wait exactly one year

questions.hint: The lesson makes a point of saying nothing here happens by itself.

level-3.title: Claiming it: tax, health and the paperwork
summary: Section 80U lets a person with a disability take a flat deduction from taxable income — ₹75,000 at 40–79%, and ₹1,25,000 where the disability is severe. It needs no bills or receipts.
Section 80DD does the same for a family member supporting a dependant with a disability. One household usually claims one or the other, not both for the same person.
Over a working life these deductions are worth a large sum, and they are among the most commonly missed.
Health cover: eligible families may come under Ayushman Bharat or a state health scheme, which pays for hospital treatment.

Some support is routed through National Trust registered organisations — caregiver help, community living, rehabilitation — but eligibility depends on which disability category applies, so check before relying on it.
Everything above is a right attached to paperwork. The order is: disability certificate, then UDID, then each scheme separately.
Rules, amounts and income limits change. Confirm the current position on the official portal or with the district social welfare office before you count on a figure.
None of this is charity. It exists because being Deaf costs money that hearing people never have to spend.

questions.prompt: A father supports his Deaf daughter, who has no income of her own. Whose tax return should claim the disability deduction, and under which section?

image.alt: A father's tax form beside his daughter's, only one with income

options.label: The father's return, under Section 80DD, since he supports a dependant with a disability
The daughter's return, under Section 80U, regardless of who supports her
Both returns can claim the full deduction separately

questions.hint: 80U is for the disabled person themselves if they have income; 80DD is for whoever supports a dependant.

questions.prompt: Section 80U requires no bills or receipts at all, yet it is among the most commonly missed deductions. What does this suggest is the real reason people miss it?

image.alt: A simple form with no receipts attached, yet often left unfiled

options.label: People likely do not know it exists or forget to claim it — not that it is hard to prove
It is missed because the paperwork is too difficult
It is missed because receipts get lost

questions.hint: If no receipts are needed, difficulty of proof cannot be the reason it gets missed.

questions.prompt: Someone tries to apply directly for Ayushman Bharat health cover using only their aadhaar card, without ever getting a disability certificate or a UDID card. What is likely to go wrong?

image.alt: An application attempted out of the usual three-step order

options.label: Most disability-linked schemes expect the certificate and UDID first — skipping them is likely to block the application
Nothing will go wrong, aadhaar alone is always enough
The order does not matter for health schemes specifically

questions.hint: Recall the exact three-step order the lesson insists on, and what usually comes first.
